title: Domain wall motion in ferromagnetic nanowires driven by a localized Gaussian thermal gradient
authors: M. A. Jafar Pikul, M. A. S. Akanda, M. T. Islam
abstract: We investigate magnetic domain wall (DW) dynamics in a uniaxial ferromagnetic nanowire under the localized Gaussian temperature profile of a laser spot using the stochastic Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation. The DW velocity increases linearly with peak laser temperature and decreases with increasing laser to DW distance. The velocity varies nonlinearly with Gilbert damping because damping strengthens thermal magnon excitation but shortens the magnon propagation length. The DW initially lies away from the laser-heated region, so the temperature gradient at its position is effectively zero and the entropic torque is negligible. The DW motion is therefore mainly driven by magnonic spin-transfer torque. We analyze laser temperature, laser to DW distance, damping, uniaxial anisotropy, and laser width. The analysis shows that laser width and laser to DW distance independently control the DW response. These findings may clarify the mechanism of localized thermally driven DW motion and guide thermal control strategies in spintronic racetrack-memory devices.
summary: This work models domain wall motion in ferromagnetic nanowires driven by localized laser heating. The simulations show that the DW velocity scales linearly with temperature but is attenuated by distance due to magnon current decay. Key findings establish that both the laser spot size and the separation distance act as independent control parameters for thermal spintronics devices.
main_problem: The study investigates how magnetic domain wall (DW) motion is driven by a localized Gaussian thermal gradient generated by a focused laser spot.
main_result: The DW velocity increases linearly with peak laser temperature and decreases as the distance from the heat source increases due to magnon current attenuation. The dynamics are controlled independently by both the laser width and the separation distance.
method: Micromagnetic simulations utilizing the stochastic Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (sLLG) equation were employed to model the time evolution of magnetization.
model_or_system: The system is a uniaxial ferromagnetic nanowire containing a head-to-head DW. The dynamics are governed by the sLLG equation under the influence of a localized Gaussian temperature profile, with motion primarily driven by magnonic spin-transfer torque ($\mu$STT).
key_observables: Translational velocity ($v$), angular velocity ($\mathrm{d}\phi/\mathrm{dt}$), and DW displacement ($\Delta x/d$).
important_parameters: Peak laser temperature ($T_L$), laser to DW distance ($d = N\sigma_L$), Gilbert damping ($\alpha$), uniaxial anisotropy ($K_u$), and laser width ($\sigma_L$).
main_assumptions: The entropic torque is negligible because the initial DW position has an effectively zero local temperature gradient, simplifying the driving mechanism to $\mu$STT.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the linear dependence of velocity on $T_L$, the decay of velocity with increasing separation distance ($N$), and non-monotonic dependencies on damping ($\alpha$) and anisotropy ($K_u$).
paper_structure: The analysis systematically varies key physical parameters—$T_L$, distance, $\alpha$, $K_u$, and $\sigma_L$—to map out the functional dependence of DW velocity and angular dynamics.
why_interesting: While focused on magnetism, the use of stochastic equations (sLLG) to model thermal fluctuations and non-equilibrium dynamics in a spatially varying field provides relevant computational techniques applicable to open quantum systems or dissipative many-body physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of the Permalloy nanowire with length 1024 nm and cross-section 8 × 8 nm2, containing a head-to- head domain wall (DW) at the center. The red curve repre- sents the localized Gaussian temperature profile, which peaks at the laser position XL. The laser spot is located at a dis- tance d = NσL to the right of the initial DW position XDW, where σL is the laser width. Blue and red coloring indicate the colder and hotter regions, respectively. The DW width ∆ and the laser to DW distance d are also indicated.

FIG. 2. Effect of laser temperature on DW dynamics for fixed N = 7 (d = 105 nm), σL = 15 nm, α = 0.001, and Ku = 2×105 J m−3. (a) Normalized DW displacement ∆x/d as a function of time for TL = 200, 250, 300, 350, 400, 500, 600, 700, and 800 K. The DW moves toward the hotter region for all temperatures, and the displacement increases with TL. (b) Translational velocity v (filled black squares) and angu- lar velocity dϕ/dt (open red circles) as functions of TL. Both quantities increase linearly with laser temperature. Error bars represent one standard deviation over 15 independent simu- lations.

FIG. 3. Dependence of DW dynamics on laser to DW dis- tance for fixed TL = 300 K, σL = 15 nm, and α = 0.001. (a) Normalized displacement ∆x/d versus time for N = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, where d = NσL. (b) Translational velocity v (filled black squares) and angular velocity dϕ/dt (open red circles) versus N. Both quantities decrease with increasing N because the magnon current weakens as it travels farther from the laser spot to the DW.

FIG. 5. Uniaxial anisotropy study for fixed TL = 300 K, N = 7, σL = 15 nm, and α = 0.001. (a) Translational veloc- ity v (filled black squares) and angular velocity dϕ/dt (open red circles) plotted against Ku. As Ku increases, v decreases while dϕ/dt increases. (b) DW width ∆plotted against Ku. Filled black circles represent values extracted from tanh fits to the simulated magnetization profiles, and the blue curve represents the analytic prediction, ∆= p

FIG. 4. Damping dependence of DW dynamics in the sub- Walker regime for fixed TL = 300 K, N = 7, σL = 15 nm, and Ku = 2 × 105 J m−3. Translational velocity v (filled black squares) and angular velocity dϕ/dt (open red circles) are plotted as functions of α (×10−3). The velocity reaches a broad maximum near α ≈0.002–0.003 and then levels off, while dϕ/dt decreases after reaching its maximum near α ≈0.002. This behavior reflects the competition between magnon generation and magnon propagation.
